newsitem.title: USA: Prodi walked with confidence at G7 summit.
newsitem.headline: Prodi walked with confidence at G7 summit.

text.p: Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi has walked with an unaccustomed swagger at a summit of world leaders in Denver as the United States praised Rome's new diplomatic role in the Balkans.

Showing a knack for survival in the rough and tumble world of Italian politics, Prodi has already achieved more than many of his predecessors simply by staying in office long enough to attend two successive Group of Seven summits.

"I came here to represent my country so that it can be taken seriously" Prodi told a news conference on Sunday at the end of the summit. "I was pleased to hear people say that for the second year running the same Italian Prime Minister is there."

The Denver conference got off to a good start for Prodi when U.S. President Bill Clinton told reporters: "I want to thank Prime Minister Prodi for the extraordinary leadership Italy has show in he Balkans."

It was a sign that Italy is starting to reap rewards for its role in Albania, where it leads a multinational military force sent to help restore order after the country descended into chaos this year.
But Prodi criticized the United States for excluding Slovenia and Romania from the first round of expansion of the NATO Western alliance.

He told a news conference on Saturday he believed the two nations should be allowed in to help stabilize NATO's volatile southeastern flank -- an area on Italy's doorstep that is causing increasing concern to Rome .
Washington surprised its allies last week by saying that only three former Warsaw Pact states -- the Czech Republic, Hungary and Poland -- should be included in the first wave of new members.
"There is a complete difference of opinion on this matter," Prodi said. "I said Mr. President (Clinton), this is a big mistake."

Underlying Italy's more confident posture -- apart from Prodi's survival in office for more than a year -- is a sense that a tough campaign to ready the country for membership of a single European currency may be paying off.

Italy has until recently been seen as a straggler in the race among European Union nations to tame public sector deficits, rein in inflation and qualify for European economic and monetary union (EMU), set for launch in 1999.

But Prodi's bid to force state finances into a tight corset is starting to show results just as Germany and France, the two front-runners to join EMU, are faltering as low growth and high unemployment drive up their budget deficits.

The Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD), a club of industrial nations, has forecast Germany, France and Italy would all run public sector deficit to gross domestic product (GDP) ratios of 3.2 percent in 1997.

That is just short of a three percent target which EMU aspirants have to meet this year to join the planned currency union in a first wave. Many now believe Italy' chances of making the grade have never been better.

The final communique at the G7 summit did not spare Italy in calling on it -- together with Germany and France -- to cut public deficits, adding "they will need to deepen structural reforms to reduce barriers to job creation."

But to the Italians, being bracketed with Germany and France was a back-handed compliment. "We were mentioned together with the French and the Germans, so what more could we want?" said an Italian summit delegate.
